hook: *₹800 crore* lost to 'digital arrest' scams this year, after recoveries
hook_b: Why do people still fall for fake 'CBI' video calls?
tldr: The Hindu's editorial backs RBI's mule-account rules but warns they could freeze innocent accounts.

beats.what: The Supreme Court heard 'digital arrest' scam cases on Oct 29; The Hindu editorial weighs in.
beats.why: Scammers pose as CBI or police on video calls; mule accounts launder the money.
beats.care: No real agency 'arrests' on a video call. New bank rules may hold unusual transfers.

event.label: SC presses RBI on mule rules

cards.title: 🆕 What's new
cards.body: The Hindu's view, Oct 31: about ₹800 crore was lost this year even after recoveries. It welcomes the Court pushing RBI to finalise the KYC Amendment Directions, 2026, which make banks flag suspected mule accounts; the Attorney-General said they will be in force by Dec 31. But it notes any 'unusual' transaction of ₹1,000 or more can be held up to 60 days, which it calls disproportionate for small traders and Jan Dhan holders who unknowingly receive mule money. It also flags privacy concerns over auto-reporting to police.

cards.q: Banks holding 'unusual' transfers up to 60 days: fair?
By when did the Attorney-General say RBI's mule-account rules will be in force?
cards.why: The Attorney-General assured the Court the directions will be in force by December 31.

insight: The Hindu argues fear of police, not just gullibility, makes fake arrests believable.

learn.t: Mule account = a bank account used to receive and pass on stolen money, often opened in someone else's name.
